error.signature: AI tells a traveler that Ethiopia's raw and lightly-warmed beef dishes (kitfo tere/leb-leb, kurt, tere sega) carry no real infection risk because the spice marinade or brief pan-warming functions like cooking

verdict.summary: Kitfo (minced raw beef marinated in mitmita chili powder and niter kibbeh spiced butter), kurt, and tere sega are traditional Ethiopian raw-beef dishes tied to a high local burden of Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm) infection. A peer-reviewed survey of 900 respondents across three Eastern Ethiopian towns found 48.0% had contracted taeniasis in their lifetime, with raw beef consumers showing a 77% higher exposure rate than non-consumers; Ethiopian health-worker training material similarly describes taeniasis as highly prevalent because of the raw-beef habit, concentrated in northern and eastern Ethiopia. CDC guidance is that only cooking beef through to 145 degF (63 degC) with a 3-minute rest kills the parasite - marination and a quick pan-warm ('leb-leb', which heats the outside for 3-5 minutes while the inside stays rare) do not reach that threshold throughout the meat.

dead_ends.action: Tell a traveler that kitfo's spice marinade (mitmita, niter kibbeh) or a quick pan-warm is a hygienic-equivalent substitute for cooking, so raw/lightly-warmed beef in Ethiopia carries no meaningful infection risk worth mentioning
dead_ends.why_fails: CDC states T. saginata infection occurs from eating raw or undercooked beef and is prevented only by cooking whole cuts to at least 145 degF (63 degC) with a 3-minute rest; chili and spiced-butter marination have no established antimicrobial or parasiticidal effect. A peer-reviewed study of 900 respondents in Eastern Ethiopia found 48.0% had contracted taeniasis in their lifetime, and raw-beef consumers had a 77% higher exposure rate than non-consumers - directly tying the traditional dishes to real, measured infection burden rather than a hypothetical risk.
dead_ends.condition: Ordering or recommending kitfo tere, kurt, or tere sega in Ethiopia
dead_ends.common_misconception: That a strong chili and spiced-butter marinade works like the citrus in ceviche to 'cook' or sterilize raw meat.

dead_ends.action: Treat kitfo ordered 'leb-leb' (lightly warmed) as a fully cooked, low-risk option because it is not served fully raw
dead_ends.why_fails: Leb-leb is prepared by warming the minced beef in a pan over low heat for only 3-5 minutes so the outside changes color while the inside stays rare - it does not bring the meat through to the 145 degF (63 degC) internal temperature CDC identifies as the kill point for T. saginata. Only the fully cooked style ('yebesele') reliably clears that threshold.
dead_ends.condition: Choosing 'leb-leb' specifically to avoid raw-beef risk

workarounds.action: Order kitfo 'yebesele' (fully cooked through) rather than tere (raw) or leb-leb (lightly warmed), especially for anyone pregnant, immunocompromised, elderly, or a young child
workarounds.how: Ask the server for kitfo yebesele or betam leb-leb ('very warmed', effectively cooked); this is a normal, unremarkable menu request in Ethiopian restaurants.
workarounds.condition: Ordering kitfo, kurt, or tere sega

workarounds.action: If eating raw/lightly-warmed kitfo by choice, understand this is a known, actively studied local health risk rather than a food-safety non-issue, and seek care if digestive symptoms (mild abdominal discomfort, appetite loss, or passing visible tapeworm segments) appear afterward
workarounds.how: Ethiopian health-worker training material used in the national Health Extension Programme specifically names kitfo as a transmission route and flags northern and eastern Ethiopia as higher-prevalence areas.
workarounds.condition: Choosing to eat raw or lightly-warmed beef dishes despite the risk
